sections.title: Two families of vowels
sections.content: Hungarian vowels split into two families — back (a, á, o, ó, u, ú) and front (e, é, i, í, ö, ő, ü, ű) — and every word belongs to one family or the other, decided by its own vowels. Suffixes come in matching versions: once you know which family a word belongs to, you already know which version of a suffix it needs. This is *vowel harmony*, and it isn't a rule you apply — it's a rule Hungarian speakers' ears enforce automatically, the way an English speaker's ear rejects "a apple" without thinking about it.

When you're not sure which family a word belongs to, check its last vowel — that one decides. *Asztal* ends in a (back), so it takes *-ok*. *Szék* ends in é (front, unrounded), so it takes *-ek*. *Sör* ends in ö (front, rounded), so it takes *-ök*. A handful of words don't play by this rule and just have to be learned — you'll meet them one at a time. Guessing wrong here is the single most common beginner slip in Hungarian, and every native speaker has heard a learner do it — it's a completely forgivable mistake, not a sign you're doing something fundamentally wrong.
